content:
If arthritis makes everyday things like washing, dressing, cooking or getting around your home hard, you can ask your local council's adult social care team for a needs assessment. It is free, anyone can ask for one, and you do not need a diagnosis of anything else or a set level of income. Describe your bad days, not your best ones: say what you cannot do, what takes much longer, what hurts, and what is unsafe. The assessment can lead to equipment, home changes, help from carers or other support, and you can complain if you disagree with the result.

This guide is for people with any kind of arthritis who are struggling at home, and for the family or friends who help them. If you mainly need a walking frame, commode or wheelchair for a short time, see borrowing equipment. If you are the person giving the care, you can also ask for a carer's assessment of your own. Money benefits such as Attendance Allowance are separate and come from the government, not the council.

What a needs assessment is

A needs assessment is how your council finds out what help you need to manage day to day. The NHS says it is free and anyone can ask for one. It is the first step before the council can arrange things such as:

  • equipment like a walking frame, perching stool, raised toilet seat or personal alarm
  • changes to your home, such as grab rails or a walk-in shower
  • practical help from a paid carer, for example with washing or dressing
  • meals at home, day centres or lunch clubs

The rules described here are for England, under the Care Act 2014. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have similar assessments with their own rules, run by councils or, in Northern Ireland, health and social care trusts. Your local council website will explain what applies where you live.

How to ask for one

  • Contact adult social care at your local council by phone or online. GOV.UK can find your council for you.
  • Someone else, such as a relative, your GP or a hospital team, can ask on your behalf if you agree.
  • If you are in hospital, ask the ward team about an assessment before you are discharged. See reablement after hospital.
  • Say clearly if things are urgent, for example if you have fallen, cannot get to the toilet safely or your carer can no longer manage.

There is no fixed waiting time. If you have not heard back, ring and ask when it will happen, and tell them if things have got worse.

Why arthritis is easy to under-describe

Arthritis often varies from day to day, and many people are used to saying they are fine. In an assessment that can mean you get less help than you need. Under the national rules in England, you count as unable to do something not only if you cannot do it at all, but also if you can only do it with help, if it causes you significant pain, distress or anxiety, if it puts you or others at risk, or if it takes you much longer than it normally would.

That matters with arthritis. If you can get dressed but it takes an hour and leaves you exhausted and in pain for the morning, say so.

How to prepare

  • Keep a diary for a week or two before the assessment: what you managed, what you could not do, how long tasks took, pain afterwards, near-misses and falls. Our activity diary guide shows a simple way to do this.
  • Think through a typical day from getting out of bed to going back to it: washing, toilet, dressing, making food and drinks, eating, taking medicines, getting around inside and outside, housework, shopping, seeing people.
  • Mention the small things. The NHS advises giving as much detail as you can, even things like turning taps on and off. Leaving things out can reduce the help recommended.
  • Describe bad days as well as good ones, and how often bad days happen.
  • Include what your carer does. If a relative quietly does your shopping, cooking or washing, the assessor needs to know, including whether they can keep doing it.
  • Have someone with you to help explain and take notes. If you have nobody and would find the process hard, you can ask the council for an independent advocate.

What happens in the assessment

A social worker, occupational therapist or other council worker will ask how you manage everyday tasks. It can happen at home, by phone or video, or through a self-assessment form. They may ask you to show them, for example, getting out of a chair or making a drink. Do it the way you normally would on an ordinary day, and stop if it hurts. If you might need adaptations, you may be referred for a separate home assessment. See what an occupational therapist can do.

After the assessment

  • You should get the result in writing. If you are eligible, the council works with you on a care and support plan.
  • Paying for care. You will usually have a financial assessment (means test) to see whether the council will pay towards care. Some help, such as assessed equipment, small adaptations and short-term reablement after hospital, is often free. Ask what you will be charged before you agree.
  • Choosing how help is arranged. You can ask for direct payments to arrange care yourself.
  • If you are not eligible, the council should still give you free advice about other help in your community, such as befriending, lunch clubs or local charities. Ask if this does not happen.
  • Things change. If your arthritis gets worse, you have a fall or your carer can no longer help, ask for a review.

If you disagree

You have a right to complain. Start with your council's complaints procedure, which should be on its website. If you are unhappy with how the council handles it, in England you can then go to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman. Age UK's advice line on 0800 678 1602 can also help.

For family and carers

  • You can request the assessment for the person you help if they agree, and you can be there.
  • Be honest about what you do and what you can sustain. The assessment is not a test of how much you can cope with.
  • Your own needs are assessed separately in a carer's assessment.

When it cannot wait

  • Call 999 after a serious fall or injury, or if someone cannot be got up safely.
  • Contact NHS 111 or your GP if someone suddenly cannot manage, becomes confused or seems very unwell, as there may be a medical cause such as an infection.
  • Tell the council it is urgent if someone is not safe at home tonight.

Common questions

Do I have to pay for the assessment?

No. The needs assessment is free. Any charges are for the care itself, after a financial assessment.

Will they take away my independence?

The aim is to help you stay as independent as possible at home. You can say what matters to you and what you want help with.

Can I have an assessment if I have savings?

Yes. Anyone can ask for a needs assessment whatever their income or savings.
